text: Thank you, Your Honor. Good morning. May it please the court. Adam Pearson for Appellant Pure Jen Holdings. The district court erred in denying Pure Jen's motion to dismiss under the TCPA. Appellee's sole asserted claim is based on allegations that Pure, among other things, orchestrated a deceptive misinformation campaign through social media and gave misleading information through public advertisements. These allegations trigger the protections under the TCPA and required Appellee Neora to present clear and convincing evidence of its claim. This it has not and cannot do, and therefore dismissal is appropriate under the TCPA. There's been no challenge to that, and it's obvious from the petition that involves speech allegedly engaged by pure. The dispute is about whether that speech relates to a public concern. I'd like to first discuss that because that is an obvious path that we think that the district court erred that triggers the protections under the TCPA. The speech at issue here, again, involves products, both Neora and Pure's products that were in the marketplace. Neora has challenged this on the fact that Pure's product, the specific product, was not specifically available for sale at the time that many of these allegations or many of these alleged speeches took place. And so it's not only Pure's products that are implicated by the speech allegations in the petition. It is also Neora's products, and there's no dispute that Neora's products were in the marketplace at the time of this speech. Secondly, there is no support in the case law that a good is not in the marketplace within the purpose of the TCPA if it's not actually for sale available yet. The Supreme Court has defined this provision of the public concern of a good in the marketplace in creative oil and gas. It states, a communication falls into this definition if it has, quote, some relevance to a wider audience of potential buyers or sellers in the marketplace, as opposed to communications of relevance only to the parties to a particular transaction. The speech here fits that definition, even if you're only looking at Pure's product. It's not disputed that Pure had begun marketing its good amongst the public through social media. It had engaged in communications with potential buyers and sellers. And that's the distinction here. Pure was not communicating with any specific buyers or sellers for a particular transaction. It was communicating to the public about a forthcoming product that was in the marketplace at the time. There has been, as this panel is well aware, an avalanche of litigation over this statute. And it's important power not just to dismiss lawsuits soon after they're filed, but also because of the automatic stay. It's that automatic stay that allows a party who defeats a motion to dismiss to be stopped in their tracks. And that's why there are so many appeals from the denial of a motion to dismiss. It's unusual in in Texas law. It's probably unusual in any law. That's why we see so many of these motions. Here, the trial court found that Neora had had. The trial court was correct in its ruling, and I look forward to exploring that further. I do think it's important to note the purpose of this statute is not just to protect citizens from retaliatory lawsuits, but also to protect the rights of a person to file a meritorious lawsuit. The other over the overarching point I'll make is that most of PURE's arguments revolve around the fact that some of the statements referenced in the petition were made publicly or because they involve business. But that is not the standard to grant PURE the right to use this powerful tool to deprive Neora of the right to pursue this claim. First and most fundamentally, the TCPA simply does not apply to this case. As everyone knows, PURE had a burden at the trial court. It had a burden to show by a preponderance of the evidence that the action was based on or in response to PURE's exercise of free speech or association, the two rights asserted here, and that the claim is factually predicated on the alleged conduct that falls within the scope of those defined rights. Importantly, we are to consider the pleadings as well as the affidavits. We don't often consider the pleadings. The Lipsky Court to Texas Supreme Court noted that with notice pleading standard, a lot of times your petition can be pretty bare bones, and especially in defamation cases where these kinds of issues arise most frequently. But between them, they have to provide enough detail to show a factual basis for the lawsuit. Here we have a detailed petition and affidavits. We know they're reviewed in the light most favorable to Neora. And as this court held in Rousier, we review that in the light most sympathetic to non-applicability. That's effectively a presumption against the applicability of this statute. We know we can't blindly accept attempts by the movement to characterize the claims as implicating protected expression. And much of the briefing in this case is just that. Very generalized statements that I will get into further. And importantly on applicability, it's important to note that PURE submitted no evidence on this problem. It's relying entirely on the petition. The first issue I'll address is free speech. We know that the statute itself says that there must be a communication and connection with a matter of public concern. The question is what is being said. It's not a question simply of whether it's public or private. The question is what is being said. Now the statute gives five examples of issues where public concern may arise. Health and safety, environmental, economic, community well-being, et cetera. Goods or services in the marketplace. Those are examples where issues of public concern may arise. But the content of the communication is the key. The content of the communication must relate to a matter of public concern. We know this is true since at least December of 2019 when the Texas Supreme Court ruled in creative oil and gas. Creative oil and gas, they made clear this very important point that a matter of public concern, the linchpin of this statute, is that the matter involves political, social, or other concern to the community. And the court made clear that types of communications in the statute don't paradoxically enlarge the concept of public concern. And went on at page 137 to note not every communication related somehow to one of the broad categories in 27017 always regards a matter of public concern. The Eastland Court of Appeals in blue gold wrote a thoughtful opinion amplifying this point about communications do not become a matter of public concern based on the nature of the business. There must be some relevance beyond the interests of the parties. This court has held likewise. It had started to reach this conclusion, I believe, in Dyer, which predates creative oil. In Dyer, the court emphasized that public concern remains the critical issue. But creative oil leaves no doubt that that is, in fact, what we do. We scrutinize the very statements in issue. Many of this court's opinions do turn on fundamentally private communications. And this case involves a backdrop, as we use the term in the petition, a backdrop of some public communications. And the key linchpin of the claim is private. But public versus private, to me, is not the cornerstone of this case, though it's interesting and the case could easily turn on it. What we know is that the subject matter must be relevant to a matter of public concern. In Goldberg versus EMR, this court noted communications about purely private economic matters. In United Development Funding, the court said not every communication relating to the broad categories regards a matter of public concern. And just recently, as we noted in our supplemental authority, the White case authored by Justice Whitehill talks about how the communication must address the subject of legitimate news interest. That is, a subject of general interest and value and concern to the public. So earlier cases have spent a lot of time looking at purely private communications about purely private business matters.
